title: B2 · L26 — Idioms: animals
description: Idiomas con animales: let the cat out of the bag, elephant in the room, hold your horses, a wolf in sheep's clothing. Recursos vivos que dan colorido y naturalidad al B2.

questions.prompt: Situación: tu hermana revela sin querer el destino de tu viaje sorpresa.
questions.question: What does 'to let the cat out of the bag' mean?
options: To finally free a pet from confinement.
To reveal a secret, usually by accident.
To deliberately spread a rumour.
To keep information strictly confidential.
questions.explanation: 'Let the cat out of the bag' significa revelar un secreto — casi siempre sin querer. OJO: no es lo mismo que 'spill the beans', que suena más deliberado. Es la idiomática típica cuando alguien arruina una sorpresa. Origen posible: mercados medievales donde estafadores vendían un 'cerdito en un saco' que resultaba ser un gato.
examples: My mum let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party — I could tell she was hiding something! → familia
Please don't let the cat out of the bag about the redundancies until we've told the team. → oficina, confidencial

questions.prompt: En una reunión de dirección, todos evitan hablar del recorte de presupuesto.
questions.question: 'The elephant in the room' refers to...
options: A physically imposing colleague who intimidates others.
An obvious problem or topic everyone deliberately avoids.
A pet-friendly office policy.
An inside joke shared by close colleagues.
questions.explanation: 'The elephant in the room' es ese tema evidentísimo que nadie se atreve a nombrar — despidos, un divorcio, un fracaso. Verbo colocado: 'address / acknowledge / ignore the elephant in the room'. Idiomática MUY común en reuniones profesionales y terapia; suena madura y directa, no agresiva.
examples: OK, let's address the elephant in the room — are we actually going to make the deadline? → meeting franca
Nobody wanted to mention the elephant in the room: Dad's drinking. → cena familiar tensa

questions.prompt: Un colega quiere responder a un cliente enojado antes de leer el email completo.
questions.statement: 'Hold your horses!' significa esperar o ir más despacio antes de actuar.
questions.explanation: VERDADERO. 'Hold your horses!' es una petición informal y ligeramente jocosa de que la otra persona espere o piense antes de saltar. Registro: coloquial, no lo uses en un email formal. Metáfora del jinete tirando de las riendas. Alternativas: 'Slow down!', 'Not so fast!'.
examples: Hold your horses — let me finish reading before you reply. → colega impulsivo
Whoa, hold your horses! We haven't even signed the contract yet. → freno en negociación

questions.text: Watch out for him — he's a wolf in sheep's clothing and definitely not to be trusted.
questions.explanation: Advertencia sobre alguien engañoso. Connected speech: 'watch out for' se fusiona en 'watch-au-fer' y 'he's a' colapsa a 'hi-zə'. Nota la /f/ suave de 'wolf' y el énfasis rítmico en 'DEF-i-nite-ly not to be TRUS-ted' — la advertencia lleva stress en las palabras clave. Origen bíblico (Mateo 7:15).
examples: That new consultant seems friendly but he's a wolf in sheep's clothing — check his references. → oficina
Be careful with her — total wolf in sheep's clothing. She smiled while stealing my client. → aviso entre amigos

questions.prompt: Estás a punto de dar una presentación importante ante el CEO.
questions.question: What does 'to have butterflies in your stomach' mean?
options: To feel physically sick from something you ate.
To feel intensely hungry before a meal.
To feel nervous or anxious in anticipation of something.
To be uncontrollably excited and happy.
questions.explanation: 'Butterflies in your stomach' describe esa sensación de nervios anticipatorios — no miedo puro, sino esa mezcla entre emoción y ansiedad. Se usa para bodas, entrevistas, primeras citas, presentaciones. Idiomática universal y muy natural. Registro neutro. Alternativa formal: 'to feel apprehensive'.
examples: I always get butterflies in my stomach right before pitching to a new client. → confesión honesta
She had butterflies in her stomach walking down the aisle — happy nerves. → boda

questions.prompt: Miras por la ventana y ves un aguacero brutal.
questions.statement: 'It's raining cats and dogs' es la forma más natural que usaría un nativo hoy en día.
questions.explanation: FALSO. Aunque todos los libros de texto la enseñan, 'raining cats and dogs' suena ANTICUADA y ligeramente cómica hoy en día. Nativos modernos prefieren: 'it's pouring (down)', 'it's chucking it down' (UK), 'it's absolutely bucketing' (UK), 'it's coming down hard' (US). Úsala solo con ironía o para hacer reír.
examples: Better cancel the picnic — it's absolutely pouring out there. → uso moderno y natural
Ha, it's raining cats and dogs, as my grandma would say. → uso irónico consciente

questions.prompt: Empareja cada inicio con su final natural (idiomas animales en contexto):

pairs.right: out of the bag about the promotion.

pairs.left: We need to address the elephant
pairs.right: in the room before it derails the project.
we haven't even seen the numbers yet.
in sheep's clothing. Read the small print.
before a job interview, no matter how prepared I am.

questions.explanation: Todos son idiomas animales de uso profesional/personal frecuente. Cada uno tiene una IMAGEN visual concreta que ayuda a memorizarlos: gato saliendo del saco (secreto), elefante ignorado (tabú), caballos frenados (esperar), lobo disfrazado (engaño), mariposas en el estómago (nervios). Idiomática viva, no fosilizada.
examples: Don't let the cat out of the bag about the merger — legal hasn't cleared it. → confidencial
It's the elephant in the room and someone has to say it. → coraje en reunión

questions.prompt: Una amiga por fin deja su trabajo tóxico y monta su propia empresa.
questions.question: What does 'to take the bull by the horns' mean?
options: To behave aggressively and lose your temper.
To confront a difficult situation directly and decisively.
To avoid a problem hoping it will resolve itself.
To act carelessly without weighing risks.
questions.explanation: 'Take the bull by the horns' = agarrar el toro por los cuernos, enfrentar algo difícil con decisión. Tiene tono ADMIRATIVO — sugiere valentía madura, no agresividad ni imprudencia. Muy usado como cumplido tras una decisión difícil. Colocaciones típicas: 'It's time to...', 'She finally decided to...'.
examples: She took the bull by the horns and finally asked for the raise she deserved. → admiración
Right, time to take the bull by the horns and have that conversation with HR. → automotivación

questions.target: I think it's time to address the elephant in the room — we can't keep ignoring the budget cuts if we want to survive next quarter.
questions.explanation: Fórmula profesional madura para introducir un tema espinoso en una reunión. Estructura: 'I think it's time to + address' suaviza la crítica con hedging. En hablado, marca pausas después de 'room' y 'quarter'. Nativos bajan ligeramente la voz al decir 'the elephant in the room' — la seriedad se comunica con el tono, no con volumen.
examples: Look, I think we need to address the elephant in the room here — the client's clearly not happy. → meeting seria
Honestly, someone has to be brave enough to address the elephant in the room. → reunión de crisis

questions.prompt: Tu jefe te lleva a una gala benéfica con smoking obligatorio.
questions.question: 'To be like a fish out of water' means to be...
options: In a familiar, comfortable environment.
In an unfamiliar situation where you feel out of place.
Extremely gifted at swimming or sport.
Physically exhausted after a long day.
questions.explanation: 'A fish out of water' = alguien fuera de su elemento, incómodo por no encajar. Metáfora visualmente potente: un pez muriendo fuera del agua. Registro conversacional. Se usa mucho para describir choques de contexto (rural/urbano, casual/formal, culturas diferentes). Distractor A es el opuesto, un típico truco de examen.
examples: I felt like a fish out of water at the black-tie gala — everyone else knew each other. → confesión
He's a total fish out of water in the countryside. He panics without wifi. → cotilleo cariñoso

questions.prompt: Tu hermano pequeño repite todo lo que haces.
questions.statement: 'To be a copycat' significa imitar acciones o estilo de otra persona, con matiz negativo o infantil.
questions.explanation: VERDADERO. 'Copycat' es el imitador — la palabra es INFANTIL en su origen (patios de colegio) pero también funciona en negocios para acusar a competidores de plagio. Verbo relacionado: 'to copy someone'. En marketing: 'a copycat product' = un producto que imita descaradamente al original.
examples: Stop being such a copycat! Choose your own outfit. → discusión entre hermanas
Their new phone is a total copycat of ours — even the box design. → queja empresarial

questions.text: You'll have to work like a dog if you want to finish this project by Friday.
questions.explanation: Aviso realista sobre carga de trabajo. Connected speech: 'you'll have to' colapsa a 'you-l-hafta' — la /h/ de 'have' es casi muda y 'have to' siempre suena /hæftə/, nunca /hæv tu/. 'Work like a dog' se pronuncia como una sola unidad rítmica: 'WORK-lai-kə-DOG'. Idiomática cotidiana en el mundo laboral.
examples: I've been working like a dog all week and I'm absolutely knackered. → queja laboral (UK)
She worked like a dog to put herself through law school. → admiración por esfuerzo

questions.prompt: Un colega te da una explicación demasiado perfecta sobre por qué faltan cuentas.
questions.question: What does 'to smell a rat' mean?
options: To have a bad head cold that affects smell.
To suspect that something dishonest or wrong is happening.
To feel disgusted by someone's behaviour.
To dislike a person on first meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Smell a rat' = intuir que algo no cuadra, oler chanchullo. Es una sospecha basada en instinto, no en pruebas. Muy usada en contextos de fraude, negociaciones sospechosas o promesas demasiado buenas. Suena investigadora, no paranoica. Distractor D confunde con 'take a dislike to someone'.
examples: Something's off about those numbers — I smell a rat. → intuición contable
When he offered 50% below market, we smelled a rat and walked away. → negociación

questions.target: I felt like a fish out of water at the corporate dinner. Everyone was talking about golf and yachts, and I don't play either.
questions.explanation: Confesión honesta post-evento social incómodo. Nota el ritmo: pausa después de 'dinner', enumeración con 'golf and yachts', y remate autoirónico con 'I don't play either'. Nativos añaden humor autodesprecatorio para no sonar quejumbrosos. Contracción 'don't' obligatoria — 'do not' sonaría rígido.
examples: Total fish out of water at the wedding — I didn't know a single person besides the bride. → anécdota casual
He felt like a fish out of water in the new city. Took him months to find his tribe. → cotilleo empático

questions.prompt: En una final de tenis nadie apostaba por la jugadora número 87 del ranking.
questions.question: What does 'a dark horse' mean?
options: A physically threatening or dangerous person.
A competitor whose hidden talents or unexpected success surprise everyone.
A very tall, imposing figure in a group.
A silent, reserved person who avoids attention.
questions.explanation: 'A dark horse' = alguien de quien nadie esperaba nada pero que sorprende positivamente. Origen: apuestas hípicas (un caballo desconocido que gana). Muy usado en política, deportes, oposiciones y también relaciones ('turned out to be a dark horse — she speaks four languages!'). Distractor D confunde con 'wallflower'.
examples: Keep an eye on the candidate from Portugal — she's the dark horse in this election. → análisis político
Turns out my quiet colleague is a total dark horse — she's climbed Everest twice. → sorpresa positiva
